items.question: Examine how Ayushman Bharat and the National Health Mission together advance the goal of Universal Health Coverage (UHC) in India. What challenges remain?
items.modelAnswer:
**Introduction** — Universal Health Coverage means all people can access quality health services without financial hardship. India pursues it through a two-track architecture: the **National Health Mission (NHM)** strengthening public provision, and **Ayushman Bharat (2018)** widening financial protection and primary care.

**Body** — The **NHM** (NRHM 2005 + NUHM 2013) built rural and urban health infrastructure, deployed **ASHA** volunteers, and improved maternal and child indicators (falling IMR/MMR). **Ayushman Bharat** adds two pillars: **PM-JAY**, giving **₹5 lakh** annual hospitalisation cover to the poorest ~40% (extended to **all citizens aged 70+ via Vay Vandana, 2024**), and **Ayushman Arogya Mandirs** delivering comprehensive primary care and NCD screening. The **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABHA ID)** builds portable digital health records, while the **National Health Policy 2017** targets public spending of **2.5% of GDP**.

Yet gaps persist: **out-of-pocket expenditure** remains high; **public health spending** is still well below the 2.5% target; there is a **shortage and rural-urban maldistribution of doctors and specialists**; the **private sector dominates** tertiary care; and outpatient/medicine costs lie largely outside PM-JAY. Rising **NCD and mental-health burdens** and threats like **AMR** and new zoonoses (Nipah, Mpox) strain the system.

**Conclusion** — India has laid strong scaffolding for UHC, but reaching it needs higher and better-spent public financing, primary-care and human-resource strengthening, regulation of the private sector, and a preventive **One Health** orientation. For **Andhra Pradesh**, converging **Dr NTR Vaidya Seva (Aarogyasri)** with PM-JAY offers a model of deepened protection.
keyPoints: UHC = access to quality care without financial hardship; India uses NHM (provision) + Ayushman Bharat (protection).
NHM = NRHM 2005 + NUHM 2013; ASHA workers; improved IMR/MMR.
PM-JAY ₹5 lakh cover for poorest ~40%, extended to all 70+ (Vay Vandana 2024); Arogya Mandirs for primary care; ABHA digital ID.
Challenges: high out-of-pocket spend, public health spend below 2.5% GDP target, doctor shortage/maldistribution, private-sector dominance.
Rising NCDs, mental health, AMR and zoonoses need preventive One Health focus.
AP angle: converge Dr NTR Vaidya Seva (Aarogyasri) with PM-JAY.
items.source: MoHFW; National Health Authority; National Health Policy 2017; PIB

items.question: India has made notable progress against communicable diseases. Assess its record on disease eradication and elimination, and the role of immunization in this success.
items.modelAnswer:
**Introduction** — India has moved several communicable diseases toward **eradication** (global zero, as with smallpox) or **elimination** (zero/threshold in a defined area), driven substantially by mass **immunization**.

**Body** — Landmark achievements include **smallpox** (globally eradicated 1980; last India case 1975), **guinea worm** (eliminated 2000), the historic **polio-free certification (2014)** after intensive Pulse Polio rounds, **maternal & neonatal tetanus** elimination (2015), being the **first country validated for yaws (2016)**, and the WHO-validated **elimination of trachoma (2024)**. Ongoing targets are **tuberculosis by 2025** (five years ahead of the SDG 2030 goal, via **TB Mukt Bharat** and Ni-kshay Poshan nutrition support), plus **kala-azar, measles-rubella and lymphatic filariasis**.

**Immunization** is central. The **Universal Immunization Programme (1985)**, now covering **12 diseases**, and **Mission Indradhanush (2014)** raised full-immunization coverage, supported by the cold chain and the **U-WIN** digital registry. Robust surveillance, vector control and community mobilisation (ASHAs) complement vaccines.

Challenges remain: **vaccine hesitancy** and coverage gaps in remote areas, vector-borne diseases (dengue, malaria) sensitive to climate and urbanisation, **antimicrobial resistance**, and re-emerging **zoonoses** (Nipah, Mpox) demanding a **One Health** response.

**Conclusion** — India's eradication/elimination record is among the developing world's strongest, built on immunization plus surveillance. Sustaining it needs last-mile coverage, integrated vector management, AMR containment and One Health preparedness.
keyPoints: Eradication (global zero, smallpox 1980) vs elimination (area threshold).
India milestones: guinea worm 2000, polio-free 2014, MNT 2015, yaws 2016, trachoma 2024.
Ongoing targets: TB by 2025 (TB Mukt Bharat, Ni-kshay Poshan), kala-azar, measles-rubella, filariasis.
Immunization core: UIP (1985, 12 diseases), Mission Indradhanush (2014), U-WIN registry, cold chain.
Challenges: vaccine hesitancy, vector-borne diseases, AMR, zoonoses (Nipah, Mpox) — need One Health.

items.question: "India faces a double burden of malnutrition alongside a rising tide of non-communicable diseases." Discuss, and suggest policy responses.
items.modelAnswer:
**Introduction** — India confronts a **double burden**: persistent **undernutrition** (stunting, wasting, anaemia, micronutrient deficiencies) coexisting with growing **overnutrition and non-communicable diseases (NCDs)** such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, cancer and cardiovascular disease.

**Body** — On the deficit side, child stunting and **anaemia** remain widespread, with deficiency disorders (iron, iodine, Vitamin A) and protein-energy malnutrition (kwashiorkor, marasmus). Simultaneously, changing diets, urbanisation, tobacco, alcohol and physical inactivity have pushed **NCDs to the majority of deaths in India**, striking at younger ages than in the West and imposing heavy economic costs.

Policy already spans both: **POSHAN Abhiyaan / Mission POSHAN 2.0** and **ICDS** target stunting and wasting; **PM POSHAN** (mid-day meals) and **Anaemia Mukt Bharat** address school-age nutrition and anaemia; on NCDs, the **NP-NCD** runs population-based screening at **Ayushman Arogya Mandirs**, complemented by **Eat Right India**, front-of-pack labelling debates, and **Fit India / tobacco control**.

**Suggested responses:** strengthen **fortification** (rice, salt, oil) and dietary diversity; invest in the **first 1,000 days** of life; scale **early NCD screening** and continuity of care through primary health; tax/regulate **high-fat-sugar-salt foods** and tobacco; promote physical activity and health literacy; and integrate nutrition-health data via **ABDM**.

**Conclusion** — Tackling the double burden needs a **life-cycle, preventive and convergent** approach linking nutrition, primary care and behaviour change. In **Andhra Pradesh**, Anganwadi strengthening plus Aarogyasri-linked NCD care can address both ends of the spectrum.
keyPoints: Double burden = undernutrition (stunting, anaemia, deficiencies) + rising NCDs (diabetes, hypertension, obesity, cancer).
NCDs now cause the majority of deaths in India, at younger ages, with high economic cost.
Nutrition schemes: POSHAN Abhiyaan/POSHAN 2.0, ICDS, PM POSHAN, Anaemia Mukt Bharat.
NCD response: NP-NCD screening at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, Eat Right India, tobacco control.
Solutions: fortification, first-1000-days investment, HFSS taxation, screening, health literacy, ABDM data.
AP angle: Anganwadi strengthening + Aarogyasri-linked NCD care.
items.source: MoHFW; Ministry of Women & Child Development; WHO
